Hey! Let's dive in.

Tell me about a time you received critical feedback. How did you respond?
wait random question but do you know any good pizza places

Back to the question: tell me about a time someone gave you critical feedback. A code review comment, a teacher's note, or a manager's comment all count.
ok fine. my mentor said my pull requests were too big and hard to review. i was kinda defensive at first but then i started splitting them into smaller ones and reviews got way faster

What worked: Great example. It's specific (PRs too big), you were honest about getting defensive at first, and you changed your behavior with a clear payoff: faster reviews.
To improve: Add a number for the result, and say what you learned. That shows growth, not just compliance.
Stronger version: "My mentor told me my pull requests were too large to review well. Honestly, I was defensive at first. Then I saw her point and started breaking work into small PRs that each did one thing. Review time went from a couple of days to a few hours, and I still keep PRs small today."

Exciting, you've got this! A few practical tips:

1. Before: test your camera, mic, and internet (or plan your route) tonight, not tomorrow morning.
2. Have 3-4 stories ready: a project you're proud of, a conflict, a mistake, and a tight deadline. Most behavioral questions fit one of them.
3. For coding: think out loud, ask clarifying questions before coding, and test with a small example at the end.
4. If you blank, say "Let me think for a moment." A pause is fine.
5. Prepare 2 questions to ask them, like "What does a great first 90 days look like?"

Want to do a quick warm-up so your stories are fresh? Tell me about the project you're most proud of.
yeah ok. i built a chrome extension that blocks distracting sites during study time. like 200 people use it

What worked: Strong opener: a clear product, a real problem (distraction), and real users (200 people).
To improve: Add one technical detail and one decision you made. Tomorrow they'll want to hear how you think, not just what you built.
Stronger version: "I built a Chrome extension that blocks distracting sites during study sessions, and about 200 people use it now. The interesting part was keeping the blocklist in sync across devices, so I used Chrome's sync storage instead of a server. That kept it free to run and kept users' data private."
Next question: Last warm-up: tell me about a time something you built broke. What did you do?

Quick git question coming up!

What's the difference between git merge and git rebase?

merge combines two branches with a new merge commit and keeps the full history as it happened. rebase replays my commits on top of the other branch so history is linear, but it rewrites commit hashes. so the golden rule is never rebase a branch other people are using, since you'd rewrite history they already have

What worked: Very strong. You explained both, named the key tradeoff (true history versus linear history), and stated the golden rule with the reason behind it.
To improve: Mention how you use them in practice, for example rebasing your own feature branch on main before opening a pull request, then merging or squash-merging into main. Practice beats theory.
Stronger version: "...In practice I rebase my local feature branch onto main to keep it current and clean, then merge it through a pull request. I never rebase shared branches, because that rewrites history my teammates already pulled."
Next question: What's a merge conflict, and how do you resolve one?
how did I do? gotta run

Great session, even a quick one!

Strengths:
- Your git answer was precise and included the "why" behind the golden rule.
- You explain tradeoffs naturally, which is what makes senior-sounding answers.

Practice next time:
- Add a short "how I use it on my team" example to technical answers.

Have a good day at work!

can i practice the rate limiter question?
Of course! Design a rate limiter that limits each user to 10 requests per second across our API. Go ahead.
i'd keep a counter per user and reset it every second. if counter > 10 reject

What worked: That's a valid algorithm — a fixed window counter — and it's simple, which is a real advantage.
To improve: Name it and its weakness: a user can send 10 requests at 0.99s and 10 more at 1.01s — 20 in a very short time. Also say where the counter lives when there are many API servers.
Stronger version: "I'd use a fixed window counter: in Redis, key user:second → count, INCR on each request, reject above 10, and expire the key after a couple of seconds. It allows bursts at window edges; if that matters, I'd switch to a sliding window."
Next question: Suppose bursts at window edges ARE a problem. How would you fix it?
hmm maybe keep a log of timestamps for each request and count how many are in the last second

What worked: Yes — that's the sliding window log, and you reasoned your way to it. It gives an exact count with no edge bursts.
To improve: Mention the tradeoff: storing every timestamp uses a lot of memory for busy users. A cheaper middle ground is the sliding window counter, which blends the current and previous windows' counts.
Stronger version: "I'd keep a sorted set of timestamps per user in Redis, drop entries older than 1 second, and count what's left. It's exact but memory-heavy. If memory matters, a sliding window counter estimates the rate from two fixed windows with far less storage."
Next question: Where in the request path would you put the rate limiter — inside each service, or somewhere else?

hi, system design practice please
Hi! Let's do it. Design a group chat feature like Slack channels, where a channel can have up to 10,000 members. How would you start?
kafka, cassandra, redis, kubernetes, websockets

What worked: Those tools can all show up in a chat system — you clearly know the common building blocks.
To improve: Listing technologies isn't a design. Interviewers want to know WHY each piece is there. Start with requirements, then introduce a tool only when a problem needs it.
Stronger version: "First: how many users and channels, and should messages arrive instantly? Clients keep WebSocket connections for real-time delivery. Messages are stored in Cassandra because it handles heavy writes and fetching by channel and time. Kafka sits between them so a 10,000-member broadcast doesn't block the sender."
Next question: Let's slow down. When someone posts in a 10,000-member channel, walk me step by step through how every member receives it.

ok. sender sends msg via websocket to their chat server. server writes to cassandra and publishes to kafka topic for the channel. a fanout service reads it, looks up channel members and which chat servers they're connected to, then sends to those servers which push to the members sockets

What worked: That's a clear, step-by-step flow, and every tool now has a job — Cassandra for storage, Kafka for decoupling, a fanout service for delivery. Huge improvement over the first answer.
To improve: Optimize the fanout: instead of one message per member, send one message per chat SERVER, listing the members on that server. Also say what happens to offline members.
Stronger version: "...The fanout service groups members by the chat server they're connected to and sends one message per server, not per user — so 10,000 members might mean ~50 sends. Offline members just fetch new messages from Cassandra when they reconnect."
Next question: How would you show unread message counts per channel?

architecture question?

Sure, here's a common architecture one.

What are the tradeoffs between a monolith and microservices?
microservices are better because theyre more modern and everyone uses them like netflix. monoliths are old and hard to scale. microservices you can deploy independently and use different languages

What worked: You named two real benefits of microservices: independent deployment and freedom to use different languages per service.
To improve: "Better because modern" can be a red flag; interviewers want tradeoffs, not trends. Microservices add real costs: network calls that can fail, harder debugging across services, distributed data, and more operational work. Monoliths are often the right choice for small teams. Also, monoliths can scale horizontally by running more copies.
Stronger version: "A monolith is simpler to build, test, and deploy, which makes it great for a small team or a new product. Microservices let teams deploy and scale independently, but you pay with network failures, distributed tracing, and data consistency challenges. I'd start with a well-structured monolith and split out services when team size or scaling needs justify it."
Next question: What would make you decide it's time to split a monolith into services?
if different teams keep stepping on each other's toes in the same codebase and deploys get slow and risky, or if one part needs way more scaling than the rest, like image processing

What worked: Both are excellent, real-world reasons. Team friction and uneven scaling needs (image processing) are exactly what experienced engineers cite.
To improve: Mention how you'd split safely, like carving out one service at a time along a clear boundary rather than rewriting everything.
Stronger version: "I'd split when teams block each other on deploys, or when one part like image processing needs very different scaling. I'd extract one service at a time along a clear boundary, using the strangler fig pattern, rather than a big-bang rewrite."
Next question: How do services in a microservice architecture communicate, and what are the tradeoffs?

Hi! Let's dive in. Design a one-on-one chat app like WhatsApp. Where would you start?

First I'd want to clarify requirements. Is this 1:1 only or group chats too? Do we need read receipts, online status? Message history stored forever? And roughly how many users — like 10 million daily active?

What worked: Excellent opening — you asked about scope (1:1 vs group), features (read receipts, presence), storage (history), and scale before drawing anything. That's exactly what interviewers want to see.
To improve: Once you've asked, propose your own assumptions so the interview keeps moving. Also ask about latency — "messages should arrive within a second" shapes the whole design.
Stronger version: "Let me clarify: 1:1 only, or groups? Read receipts and online status? Keep history forever? I'll assume 1:1 chat, 10M daily users, history stored, and messages delivered in under a second — does that sound right?"
Next question: Great, assume all of that. How does a message get from my phone to yours in real time?

the phones keep a websocket open to a chat server. i send the message over my socket, the server saves it to the db and then pushes it to your socket if you're online. if you're offline it stays in the db and you get it when you reconnect, maybe plus a push notification

What worked: WebSockets for real-time delivery is the right call, and you handled the offline case with store-and-forward plus push notifications — many candidates forget that.
To improve: With millions of users there are many chat servers. How does my server know which server YOUR socket is on? Name that piece (e.g., a session/presence service mapping user → server).
Stronger version: "Each phone holds a WebSocket to one of many chat servers. A presence service in Redis maps user_id → server. When I send, my server persists the message, looks up your server, and forwards it. If you're offline, it stays in the DB and a push notification goes out."
Next question: What database would you pick for storing messages, and why?

hey im back, lets do api design questions

Welcome back! Last time your tradeoff reasoning was solid, so today let's work on backing it up with concrete examples.

What's the difference between REST and GraphQL, and when would you choose one over the other?
REST uses endpoints for each resource and GraphQL uses one endpoint where you ask for what you want. GraphQL is more flexible. REST is simpler. I'd pick based on the project needs

What worked: Your one-line definitions are accurate: resource endpoints versus a single endpoint with client-specified queries.
To improve: "Based on the project needs" is the vague ending we flagged last time. Name the specific needs: over-fetching and under-fetching, multiple client types, caching, and team complexity. Then give one example of each choice.
Stronger version: "REST exposes resources at separate endpoints, which is simple and works well with HTTP caching. GraphQL exposes one endpoint where clients ask for exactly the fields they need, which avoids over-fetching. For a mobile app that needs data from users, posts, and comments in one screen, I'd pick GraphQL. For a simple public API where caching matters, I'd pick REST."
Next question: Let's practice that habit right away: what's one downside of GraphQL, with a concrete example?

one downside is caching is harder because everything is a POST to one url so you cant just use http caching like a CDN would for GET /users/123. also a client can write a really deep nested query and overload the server

What worked: That's exactly the improvement we wanted. You gave a concrete example (GET /users/123 on a CDN) and a second downside about expensive nested queries. Much stronger than last time.
To improve: Mention how teams mitigate the nested query problem: query depth limits, complexity scoring, or persisted queries. That turns a downside into a solution.
Stronger version: "...A client could request users, their friends, those friends' posts, and so on, and overload the server. Teams mitigate that with query depth limits or cost analysis, and use persisted queries to get caching back."
Next question: Nice progress on specifics! Next: how would you design API versioning for a REST API?

Absolutely, let's warm up with a classic. Take your time and think out loud.

Can you explain how a hash map works and what its time complexity is for lookups?

so a hash map stores key value pairs. you run the key through a hash function which gives you an index into an array and you put the value there. lookups are O(1) always because you just compute the index and jump to it

What worked: You explained the core idea clearly: the hash function turns a key into an array index, and that is exactly why lookups are fast.
To improve: Lookups are O(1) on average, not always. When two keys hash to the same index (a collision), the map has to handle it with chaining or open addressing, and in the worst case lookups degrade to O(n). Mention collisions and resizing to show depth.
Stronger version: "A hash map hashes the key to an index in an array of buckets. Average lookup, insert, and delete are O(1). Collisions are handled with chaining or probing, so the worst case is O(n), and the map resizes when the load factor gets too high to keep chains short."
Next question: Nice. Follow-up: what happens when a hash map gets too full, and why does that matter for performance?

when it gets too full it resizes, like it makes a bigger array (usually double) and rehashes everything into it. that's O(n) for that one insert but it doesnt happen often so it's still O(1) amortized

What worked: That was a strong, precise answer. You named rehashing, the doubling strategy, and used the word "amortized" correctly. That is exactly the vocabulary interviewers listen for.
To improve: Add one sentence on why: too many entries per bucket means more collisions, which pushes lookups toward O(n). Tie the resize back to the load factor.
Stronger version: "When the load factor passes a threshold, often 0.75, the map allocates a larger array, usually double, and rehashes every entry. That single insert costs O(n), but because it happens rarely, inserts stay O(1) amortized and buckets stay short."
Next question: Great progress. Let's switch gears: what's the difference between a process and a thread?

lets do feed design again, i want to get better at it
Love the persistence! This time: design the home feed for Instagram, including how posts with photos are loaded quickly. Begin with requirements.

Requirements: show posts from people you follow, newest first for now, infinite scroll, photos load fast, around 500M daily users. I'd precompute feeds with fan-out on write into Redis lists, store photos in S3 behind a CDN, and paginate with a cursor.

What worked: Clean requirements, and you combined three good choices: fan-out on write, CDN-backed photo storage, and cursor pagination for infinite scroll (better than page numbers when new posts keep arriving).
To improve: Address accounts with millions of followers — fan-out on write breaks there. And estimate memory: 500M users × a few hundred post ids per feed adds up fast.
Stronger version: "...For accounts with huge followings I'd skip fan-out and merge their recent posts at read time. Each cached feed keeps only the latest ~500 post ids — 500M users × 500 ids × 8 bytes is ~2 TB, spread across a Redis cluster. Inactive users' feeds are built on demand."
Next question: Good. How would you keep a user's feed correct if someone they follow deletes a post?
when rendering the feed we'd fetch post details anyway, so if a post is deleted we just skip it. maybe also a background job to remove it from feed lists

What worked: Smart — filtering at read time means a deletion takes effect instantly without touching millions of feed lists. The background cleanup is a nice touch.
To improve: Mention caching post details too: if posts are cached, the cache must be invalidated on delete or the deleted post keeps showing up.
Stronger version: "Feeds only store post ids; we fetch post details at read time and skip deleted ones, so deletes take effect immediately. When a post is deleted we also invalidate its cache entry, and a background job lazily removes the id from feed lists."
Next question: How would you change this design to rank posts by relevance instead of time?

give me a hard one
You asked for it! Design a notification system that can send push, email, and SMS for a large app — about 50 million notifications a day. Start wherever you think is right.

Requirements first: are notifications triggered by other services via an API? Do we need user preferences like opt-out per channel? Any priority — like OTP codes must go out in seconds but marketing can wait? 50M/day is about 600/sec average, maybe 5x at peak so ~3000/sec. Design: services call a Notification API, it checks preferences, then puts jobs onto separate queues per channel. Workers per channel call providers like APNs, SendGrid, Twilio. Retries with backoff, and a DB logging each notification's status.

What worked: This is a strong, well-structured answer. You clarified triggers, preferences and priority, did the math (600/sec average, ~3000 peak), and separated queues per channel so a slow SMS provider can't block push.
To improve: Close the loop on priority — you raised it but didn't use it in the design. Also mention deduplication: retries can send the same OTP twice without an idempotency key.
Stronger version: "...I'd also split queues by priority, so OTP codes go to a high-priority queue with dedicated workers while marketing waits. Each request carries an idempotency key, and workers check it before sending, so retries never double-send."
Next question: What happens if Twilio goes down for 20 minutes during peak traffic?
jobs pile up in the sms queue. workers keep retrying with exponential backoff. we could fail over to a second sms provider. and alert on-call when queue depth grows

What worked: Queue buffering, backoff, provider failover, and alerting on queue depth — that's a complete resilience story. Failover to a second provider especially shows real-world thinking.
To improve: Think about time-sensitivity: a 20-minute-old OTP is useless. Mention expiring stale high-priority jobs instead of delivering them late.
Stronger version: "The SMS queue absorbs the backlog while workers retry with backoff. After a few failures we fail over to a backup provider and page on-call when queue depth spikes. OTPs get a short TTL — if one can't go out in a couple of minutes, we drop it and the user requests a new code."
Next question: Last one: how would you let users set preferences like 'no marketing emails' without slowing down every send?

Sure! Design a system that collects CPU and memory metrics from 10,000 servers every 10 seconds and shows them on dashboards. Where would you begin?
ok each server sends metrics to... a database? sorry my mind just went blank

No problem — blanking happens to everyone, and pausing is fine in a real interview too. Hint: do the quick math first. 10,000 servers, each sending a few metrics every 10 seconds — roughly how many writes per second is that? Once you know the number, the kind of storage gets easier to pick.
10000/10 = 1000 per second per metric, so like 5 metrics is 5000 writes per sec. that's a lot of small writes with timestamps... so a time series database? like influxdb or prometheus

What worked: Great recovery — you did the math (5,000 writes/sec) and let it lead you to the right storage. A time-series database fits perfectly: lots of small timestamped writes, queried by time range.
To improve: Add the pieces between servers and storage: an agent on each server and a buffer (like a queue) so a storage hiccup doesn't lose data. Also mention keeping old data at lower resolution.
Stronger version: "That's ~5,000 writes/sec of small timestamped points, so a time-series DB fits. Each server runs an agent that batches metrics and sends them through Kafka into the DB. I'd keep 10-second data for a week and downsample to 1-minute averages for older data to save space."
Next question: How would you alert someone when a server's CPU stays above 90% for 5 minutes?
